issues.legal_issue: A property award that uses language of full ownership creates an absolute religious dedication when the award as a whole shows that the property was reserved for the institution and the named holder was given possession and management for its benefit.
material_facts: A registered partition award used language conveying the property together with all rights and interests of proprietorship to one co-sharer.
The award immediately stated that the grant was for specified purposes, including the expenses and upkeep of a temple.
It provided that, if the co-sharer failed to carry out those purposes, another co-sharer could take possession and continue the temple work.
The award denied the co-sharers and the named holder rights over the property, prohibited its transfer, and stated that it was reserved permanently for the stated purposes.
issues.conclusion: The award created an absolute dedication of the property to the temple; the named co-sharer received possession and management as its manager and trustee, not absolute ownership.
issues.legal_principle: A document must be construed as a whole to ascertain intention, considering its words in their context and the circumstances of their use. Words such as “Malik” and “Milkiyat” ordinarily raise a presumption of full ownership, but that presumption may be displaced by the context. An attempt to restrict an estate that is plainly absolute is ordinarily repugnant, but restrictions that are primary and consistent with the document’s tenor may displace the presumption. An effort should be made to read provisions harmoniously; where they irreconcilably conflict, the earlier absolute disposition prevails over later restrictions. The Court relied on Sahebzada Mohd. Kamgar Shah v. Jagdish Chandra Rao Dhabal Deo, Lalit Mohan Singh Roy v. Chukkun Lal Roy, Mst. Surajmani v. Babi Nath Ojha, Sarjoo Bara Devi v. Jyotirmoyee Debi, Mohamed Shamsool v. Shewukram, and Rai Bajrang Bahadur Singh v. Thakurain Bakhtrai Kuer.

rule.if: property_award_construction_dispute and ownership_language_used and temple_purpose_stated and (management_for_temple_provided or transfer_restricted) and property_reserved_for_temple

predicates.property_award_construction_dispute: The proceeding concerns how an award disposing of property is to be construed.
predicates.ownership_language_used: The award uses language that, read alone, indicates that a person receives full ownership of the property.
predicates.temple_purpose_stated: The award states that the property is granted for purposes benefiting a temple.
predicates.management_for_temple_provided: The award provides for a person to possess or manage the property to carry out the temple purposes.
predicates.transfer_restricted: The award restricts the transfer of the property by the person given possession or management.
predicates.property_reserved_for_temple: The award states that the property is reserved for the temple purposes.

issues.definition: When a property award uses ownership language but its stated purposes and consistent provisions reserve the property for a temple and provide for temple management or restrict transfer, the output is an absolute temple dedication.

issues.legal_issue: Owners may validly dedicate property to a religious institution through a partition award when the arbitrators make the award with the owners’ consent and on their behalf.
material_facts: The partition award’s dedication provisions were made with the consent of and at the instance of all the co-sharers.
The Panchas acted on behalf of the owners, who had the right to dedicate the property.
issues.conclusion: The dedication made through the partition award was valid because the Panchas’ act was the act of the owners, who had full authority to dedicate the property.
issues.legal_principle: An award made by arbitrators with the owners’ consent and at their instance is, for this purpose, the act of the owners. Owners with full rights in the property may make a valid dedication to a deity.

predicates.dispute_over_dedication_through_partitio: The proceeding concerns whether a religious dedication made through a partition award is valid.
predicates.award_made_with_owners_consent: The arbitrators made the dedication provisions with the owners’ consent and at their instance.
predicates.owners_had_authority_to_dedicate: The owners had full authority over the property to make a dedication.

issues.definition: When a proceeding concerns a dedication through a partition award and the arbitrators acted with the consent of owners who had authority to dedicate, the output is that the dedication through the award is valid.

issues.legal_issue: A later compromise award made by former owners cannot undo an absolute dedication that has already been made and has not been set aside.
material_facts: A registered partition award had made an absolute dedication of the property to a temple.
A later dispute over the earlier award was settled through a compromise and a further award that treated the property as belonging to a family subject to a temple-expense obligation.
The earlier award was not set aside by the court.
The later award was made after the dedication, when the former owners no longer had legal authority to go behind it.
issues.conclusion: The later award had no legal effect on the dedication already made.
issues.legal_principle: Once an absolute dedication has been made, the former owners have no legal authority to revoke or alter it. A later award or compromise cannot affect the dedication where the earlier award was not set aside; the Court also observed that the later award proceeded on the basis that the earlier award was valid.

predicates.dispute_over_later_award_and_prior_absol: The proceeding concerns whether a later award affects an earlier absolute dedication.
predicates.later_award_made_after_dedication: The later award was made after the property had already been absolutely dedicated.
predicates.prior_award_not_set_aside: A court had not set aside the award that made the prior dedication.

issues.definition: When a later award is challenged as affecting an earlier absolute dedication, and the dedication preceded the later award while the original award remains in force, the output is that the dedication remains effective.

issues.legal_issue: Subsequent conduct in dealing with property cannot alter the effect of a clear instrument that makes an absolute dedication.
material_facts: The partition award clearly and unambiguously dedicated the property to a temple.
The property’s income was credited to an account maintained for general family expenses, and the property was alienated.
The Court found that such conduct could not change the absolute dedication made by the award.
issues.conclusion: The subsequent dealings with the property and its income did not change or weaken the absolute dedication.
issues.legal_principle: Where the instrument itself is clear and unambiguous, the parties’ course of conduct is not relevant to its construction and cannot change the force or validity of the dedication it records.

predicates.religious_property_instrument_dispute: The proceeding concerns the effect of an instrument dedicating property to a religious institution.
predicates.instrument_clearly_dedicates_property: The instrument clearly and unambiguously dedicates the property to the religious institution.
predicates.later_conduct_treats_property_as_family_: After the instrument, a person dealt with the property or its income as though it belonged to the family.

issues.definition: When a religious-property dispute involves a clear instrument of dedication, later treatment of the property as family property does not change the dedication.
